newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Post-war Guatemala must bury hatreds.
newsitem.headline: Post-war Guatemala must bury hatreds.

text.p: Guatemala began its post-war era on Monday facing the enormous challenge of burying a history of fratricidal hatred and overcoming deep scepticism about its future after 36 years of guerrilla war.
"The problem with Guatemala is that civil war has become almost institutionalized," a western diplomat said.

Guatemalans turned out in the tens of thousands on Sunday to witness the end of one of Latin America's most enduring and brutal conflicts in which 100,000 people died and some 40,000 "disappeared" in counterinsurgency sweeps.

The scale of the devastation, mostly suffered during the years of military dictatorship in the 1960s-1980s, meant the celebration was more reflective than euphoric, and many -- particularly on the left -- were openly sceptical.

Before both sides effectively halted military operations last March, conflict had long been pocketed in the remote highlands, home mostly to Indians that make up a downtrodden majority in the Central American country.
Ideological frictions still run deep.
"In terms of the political polarisations that have been created over the past 36 years, they are wounds which will take a long time to heal," the diplomat said.

Putting their signature on the "Firm and Lasting Peace" treaty late on Sunday in the National Palace, President Alvaro Arzu, leaders of National Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) and U.N. Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali all spoke somberly of the hard road ahead.

The Guatemalan government has spent months on the hunt for international funds, having made expansive financial commitments in the accords to fund infrastructure projects, education, health and social programmes.

It estimates its peace bill at some $2.5 billion, more than the country's entire $2 billion foreign debt and a sizeable chunk of Gross Domestic Product, which is $14 billion. It hopes to get the bulk of that from foreign donors.

But diplomats say Arzu must also drastically raise tax revenues at home to pay his share, and they note that in his first year in office he appeared to shy away from clamping down on his main support base -- the right-wing business sector.

In a country where some 80 percent of the population -- mostly the Mayan Indians -- live in poverty, the specter of demobilized soldiers and rebel fighters pounding the streets in search of scarce jobs seems sure to increase social pressures.

Already poverty and rising crime are the main concerns of Guatemalans, many of whom had long put the war behind them. Some 15,000 soldiers and 1,700 rebels are due to be demobbed as part of the treaty.

Locals express fears that former fighters will form armed extortion and kidnap gangs. Already one small rebel faction in the western state of Queztaltenango has reportedly expressed opposition to the peace treaty and bandits dressed like rebels have recently appeared along the South coast.
One programme that the United States has pledged to support is modernisation of the corrupt and inefficient justice system, one of the biggest challenges for Guatemala.

Under the peace accords, it will be up to Guatemala's courts to resolve cases of human rights violations, and no one is sure the court system, long known for bouncing such cases from judge to judge, can handle the burden of trying war-related crimes.
Reports of human rights abuses have dropped recently, but justice remains scarce for victims.

Years of military terror, followed by the broken promises of weak civilian presidents, have fostered a profound scepticism in Guatemalan society and many on the left worry that even the URNG rebels may have sold out for peace.
According to a poll last week in Guatemala's leading daily, Prensa Libre, 78 percent of Guatemalans approved of the peace treaty, but only 38 percent believed it would be respected.

President Arzu, who has won broad acclaim at home and abroad for swiftly ending the war, when for five years his predecessors struggled to make even minor breakthroughs, says such pessimism is one of the main obstacles in the future.
"It doesn't make any sense to reach peace, which is the end of a generalized conflict, if everyone continues with their private wars," he told a news conference on Monday.
